title: He Knew They'd Kill It. Diljit Dosanjh Released Satluj Anyway — and India Pulled It in 48 Hours.
excerpt: The most controversial Indian film in years dropped without warning on ZEE5, told the story of a murdered Sikh activist, and vanished before the weekend was over. For NRIs, it's still streaming.
body:
They didn't promote it. Didn't drop a trailer countdown. Didn't tease release dates on Instagram. On the night of July 3, **Satluj** simply appeared on **ZEE5** — uncut, uncensored, and loaded with the kind of history that powerful people in India have spent three decades trying to bury.

Two days later, it was gone.

**Diljit Dosanjh** didn't flinch. Speaking to fans on Instagram Live from overseas, still in a different time zone, he said what everyone already suspected: *"This was expected from day one. If we had announced the release and promoted it two days prior, it wouldn't have been released at all."*

He even predicted the timing. *"I thought it would be banned on Monday when the offices open,"* he said, adding that the weekend removal caught him only slightly off guard. The implication was unmistakable: the machinery of censorship runs on autopilot. The only question was how fast it would catch up.

## The Story They Tried to Erase

Directed by **Honey Trehan**, *Satluj* — originally titled *Punjab '95* — is the story of **Jaswant Singh Khalra**, a Sikh human rights activist who blew the lid off one of India's darkest cover-ups. In the early 1990s, Khalra documented the illegal cremation of thousands of unidentified bodies in Punjab — people who had been detained by police and never seen again. His investigation linked the disappearances to extrajudicial killings carried out during the Punjab insurgency era that followed Operation Blue Star and the anti-Sikh violence of 1984.

For telling the truth, Khalra paid with his life. He was abducted in September 1995. His body was never found. In 2005, four Punjab Police officers were convicted for his kidnapping and murder — initially sentenced to seven years, later increased to life imprisonment.

The Central Board of Film Certification wanted **127 cuts** — erasing references to real locations, real events, real killings. Both Trehan and Dosanjh refused. The film sat with the censor board for over three years, unable to reach theaters, unable to reach audiences. Until someone at ZEE5 decided to just... put it up.


> "You can trouble me as much as you want. I am with Punjab till the day I die." — Diljit Dosanjh, Instagram Live

## The Fallout

The removal ignited exactly the kind of response you'd expect. Former Punjab Chief Minister **Sukhbir Singh Badal** called it *"an assault on our collective memory, truth, and freedom of expression."* Rajya Sabha MP and RTI activist **Saket Gokhale** wrote directly to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, demanding answers. The **Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee** urged young people to seek out and watch the film.

And in the sacred spaces, the film took on a life of its own. Diljit shared that *Satluj* was being screened inside **gurdwaras**. *"I saw a video where the film is being screened inside a Gurdwara Sahib,"* he said. *"So now I am satisfied that the film has reached you."*

He then did something extraordinary: he told fans to share their downloaded copies. *"Now you can share it among yourselves, it's your film. Once anything lands online, it never gets deleted."

*

## For the Diaspora, the Film Is Still There

Here's the detail that matters most if you're reading this from New York, London, Toronto, or Melbourne: **Satluj is still streaming on ZEE5 Global.** The ban applies only within India's borders. For the millions of Punjabi diaspora viewers worldwide — many of whom emigrated during or in the aftermath of the very period the film depicts — the film remains accessible.

ZEE5 has issued a careful statement, thanking audiences for the *"overwhelming response"* and saying the platform *"firmly stands with the film."* It also promised to *"explore all appropriate legal avenues to bring it back"* to Indian viewers, but set no timeline.

## What This Really Means

*Satluj* isn't just a film. It's a test — of whether India's streaming platforms, the last refuge for stories too uncomfortable for theaters and too true for censors, can hold their ground when the pressure arrives. ZEE5 blinked, even if it claims otherwise.

But Diljit already knew the outcome before he hit upload. He spent five and a half years getting this story made — a year and a half just to start filming, another four wrestling the censor board. He didn't need it to last on a platform. He needed it to land.

And it landed. In living rooms, on phones, and inside gurdwaras across Punjab. In 48 hours, a film about a man who was silenced reached more people than the censors ever wanted. The irony writes itself.
author: Diaspora Desk
